title: Documentation & Quality Records
shortDescription: SOP, policy, procedure, form, record — the exact vocabulary accreditation assessors use, and the one comparison (document vs record) that trips up almost everyone.
genZNote: If it isn't written down and controlled, as far as an assessor is concerned, it didn't happen.

sections.heading: Documentation Vocabulary
bullets: Policy — a high-level statement of intent set by management.
Procedure / SOP — the defined way an activity is actually carried out, step by step.
Work instruction — finer detail for a specific task, beyond what the SOP covers.
Form — a blank template used to capture information during work.
Document control — the system ensuring only the current, approved version of any document is in circulation.
Revision and approval — controlled changes to a document, each approved before use.
Distribution — ensuring the right people have access to the current version.
Obsolete documents — superseded versions, which must be clearly marked/removed from active use (though sometimes retained for historical reference).
Retention — how long records must be kept, per the applicable requirement.
Traceability — the ability to trace a result or decision back through the records that produced it.

rows: Describes HOW something should be done (policy, SOP, work instruction, blank form)
Provides EVIDENCE of what was actually done (a completed form, a signed report, a calibration certificate)
Can be revised and re-approved over time
Once created, is not edited — corrections are made through defined, traceable methods, not by altering the original
Subject to record control (retention, protection, retrievability)

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: A document describes how something should be done and is version-controlled; a record is the evidence of what was actually done and, once created, is preserved rather than edited.
keyFacts: Document control ensures only the current approved version is in circulation.
A record, once created, is not edited — corrections follow a defined, traceable method.
Retention periods for records are set by the applicable accreditation requirement, not chosen arbitrarily by the lab.
Traceability means a result or decision can be traced back through the chain of records that produced it.
commonConfusion: A 'form' and a 'record' look identical once filled in, but they are conceptually different: the blank form is a controlled DOCUMENT; the completed form becomes a protected RECORD.

highYieldFacts: Documents are revised and re-approved; records, once made, are preserved rather than edited.
A completed form is a record; the blank template is a document.
commonTraps: Editing a record directly to fix a mistake, instead of using a controlled correction method that preserves the original entry.
mustRemember: Document → describes how. Record → evidence of what was actually done.

confusedTerms.distinction: A document (policy, SOP, form) describes how something should be done and can be revised. A record is evidence of what was actually done, and once created is preserved rather than edited.

possibleQuestions: Explain the difference between a document and a record, using an SOP and a completed test report as examples.

sources.name: NABL — National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories

comparisons.distinction: A document describes HOW something should be done and can be revised (policy, SOP, blank form). A record is evidence of WHAT was actually done and, once created, is preserved rather than edited.

questions.prompt: A completed, signed calibration certificate for a piece of equipment is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: It's evidence of what was actually done — a record, not a revisable document.

questions.prompt: Which of these IS revised and re-approved over time, unlike a record?
questions.explanation: An SOP is a document — subject to version control and re-approval as procedures change.
